title: Finding the loop, and what became of it
objective: By the end of this lesson you can locate a loop in disassembly in seconds, explain loop rotation and why compilers do it, and recognise a vectorised loop from its instructions.

blocks.text: A loop is the easiest structure to find in a disassembly and one of the hardest to be sure you have understood, because the shape the compiler produces is usually not the shape you wrote.

blocks.caption: The only structural signature a loop has
lines: A backward jump. That is all.
jne  .Lbody          <-- a jump BACKWARD to it
In objdump output with addresses, look for a jump whose target address
is LOWER than the jump's own address:
/* Everything between the target and the jump is the loop body. This one
test finds every loop in any binary, regardless of what the source
said or which language it was written in. */

blocks.text: The test moved to the bottom

blocks.caption: A while loop compiled at -O1
lines: int w_loop(const int *a, long n) { int s=0; long i=0; while (i<n) { s+=a[i]; i++; } return s; }
add  eax, dword ptr [rdi + 4*rcx] ; s += a[i]
jne  .Lbody                       ; the TEST, at the BOTTOM
/* The source tests at the top; the binary tests at the bottom, with a
separate guard for the zero-iteration case. One branch per iteration
instead of two, and the bottom branch is taken every time but the last,
which is exactly the pattern a predictor learns immediately. */

blocks.title: Loop rotation
blocks.text: A while loop tests before each iteration. Compiled directly that means a test and a backward jump every time round — two branches per iteration. Rotating the loop moves the test to the bottom and hoists a single guard above the loop, giving one branch per iteration. The guard runs once; the body's branch is taken every time except the last. This is why nearly every compiled loop looks like a do-while regardless of what the source said.

rows: One branch per iteration instead of two
The same, with init before the guard
for is while with the pieces rearranged
It always runs at least once, so no guard is needed

blocks.text: The third row is why a do-while sometimes produces smaller code than the equivalent while: the guard is genuinely unnecessary. When a loop's count is known to be at least one, writing it as do-while tells the compiler something it may not be able to prove.
Loops that are not there any more

headers: What you see instead of a loop
rows: The loop had a closed form and the compiler used it
A call to memcpy, memset or strlen
The loop was recognised as a standard operation
The same body repeated several times
xmm registers and instructions ending in d, q, b or w

blocks.title: The second row surprises people
blocks.text: A hand-written loop that walks a string counting characters can compile into a call to the library strlen. The compiler recognised the idiom and substituted a routine that is faster than anything the loop would have produced. If you are looking for your loop and find a call instead, this is why — and it is a reason to check the disassembly before concluding that a hand-written version beat the library.

blocks.caption: The same three-line loop at a higher optimisation level
lines: The SAME loop compiled at -O2 instead of -O1:
movabs  rcx, 9223372036854775800      ; n rounded down to a multiple of 8
pxor    xmm0, xmm0                    ; two vector accumulators
paddd   xmm1, xmm0                    ; combine the two accumulators
pshufd  xmm0, xmm1, 238               ; then fold 4 lanes down to 1
/* Three lines of C became 111 lines of assembly: a length check, a vector
loop handling eight elements per iteration with two accumulators, a
horizontal reduction to add the lanes together, and a scalar tail. */

blocks.text: Four features identify a vectorised loop on sight: xmm or ymm registers, instructions whose names end in a size letter such as paddd, a length check before the loop deciding whether vectorising is worthwhile, and a scalar tail afterwards for the elements that did not fill a full vector. Once you recognise the shape, the size letter tells you the element type — paddd is packed add of doublewords, so four 32-bit integers at a time in a 128-bit register.

blocks.title: Two accumulators, again
blocks.text: The vector loop uses xmm0 and xmm1 as separate accumulators and adds them together at the end. That is exactly the dependency-chain-breaking technique the architecture course measured at four times the throughput. Here the compiler applied it without being asked — for integers, where regrouping is exact. For floating point it would need permission, because regrouping changes the result.

blocks.title: Watch a loop change shape
steps: Write a loop summing an int array and compile it at -O0, -O1 and -O2
Count the instructions in the loop body at each level
At -O1, identify the guard, the body and the bottom test
At -O2, find the vector loop, the length check and the scalar tail
Rewrite the loop as a do-while and see whether the guard disappears
Write a loop that copies bytes from one buffer to another and look for a memcpy call
Write a loop whose result has a closed form and confirm the loop vanishes
For each backward jump you find, state what its loop body does in one sentence
blocks.expected: A body that shrinks and then explodes: -O0 verbose, -O1 tight and scalar, -O2 long because it contains three versions of the same loop. That last observation is worth keeping — more assembly does not mean slower. The -O2 version is longer precisely because it handles the common case eight elements at a time.

cheatsheet: A loop's only signature is a backward jump: a target address lower than the jump's own
Everything between the target and the jump is the loop body
Compilers rotate loops: guard above, test at the bottom, one branch per iteration
This is why compiled while loops look like do-while loops
A do-while needs no guard, so it can produce slightly smaller code
A loop replaced by imul and shifts had a closed form
A loop replaced by a call was recognised as memcpy, memset or strlen
Vectorisation signs: xmm registers, size-suffixed names like paddd, a length check, a scalar tail
paddd is packed add of doublewords: four 32-bit integers at once
Vector loops use several accumulators for the same reason scalar code should

checkpoint.prompt: How do you find every loop in a disassembly?

choices.C: Look for a jump whose target address is lower than the jump's own address

checkpoint.explanation: A backward jump is the only structural signature a loop has, and it works regardless of source language or optimisation level.

checkpoint.prompt: A while loop compiles with a guard at the top and the test at the bottom. Why?

choices.A: Testing at the bottom gives one branch per iteration instead of two

checkpoint.explanation: The guard handles the zero-iteration case once. This is loop rotation. It is why nearly every compiled loop resembles a do-while regardless of what the source said.

checkpoint.prompt: You see xmm registers, paddd, a cmp against 8 before the loop, and a second scalar loop after it. What is this?

choices.A: A vectorised loop: the check decides whether vectorising is worthwhile, the vector body handles several elements per iteration, and the tail finishes the remainder

checkpoint.explanation: All four features together are the signature. paddd is packed add of doublewords — four 32-bit integers per instruction.

checkpoint.prompt: You look for your hand-written character-counting loop and find a call to strlen instead. What happened?

choices.C: strlen was inlined into the loop
choices.D: The compiler recognised the idiom and replaced the loop with the library routine

checkpoint.explanation: Idiom recognition is routine at higher optimisation levels. It is also a reason to check the disassembly before claiming a hand-written version beat the library.
